#4340. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4339. Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space

For the first time, a robot has successfully assembled part of a structure in space without astronauts, demonstrating a technology that could dramatically change how large spacecraft and scientific instruments are built.

The robotic system was developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). It is part of DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program, an initiative exploring ways to manufacture and assemble enormous structures directly in space.

Rather than relying on astronauts to connect individual pieces, the robot uses an automated arm to retrieve structural tubes and connecting joints from nearby storage dispensers. It then joins the components into repeating sections, called bays, that form a larger supporting framework known as a truss.

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," says Sergio Pellegrino, the Joyce and Krent Kresa Professor of Aerospace and Civil Engineering, the Lynn Booth and Kent Kresa Department of Aerospace Leadership Chair, the executive officer for aerospace, and a senior research scientist at JPL, which Caltech manages for NASA.

A Historic Step Toward Building Giant Structures in Space

Pellegrino leads Caltech's Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA) demonstration. The robotic system has spent six months in orbit attempting to construct a reflector antenna measuring 1.4 meters across. Its design combines composite fiber tubes, aluminum connectors, and a lightweight reflective surface made from Kapton, a durable polymer film commonly used in spacecraft.

DARPA compares the assembly process to building with sophisticated versions of K'Nex or Tinkertoy construction toys. However, making a robot perform those same tasks reliably in the harsh environment of space presents a far greater engineering challenge.

The team encountered technical difficulties and scheduling constraints that prevented it from finishing the entire antenna. Nevertheless, the robot successfully assembled an initial section, providing evidence that this construction method can work in orbit. Researchers believe the same basic approach could eventually support much larger frameworks carrying enormous reflective surfaces.

The orbital experiment represents the third stage of DARPA's research program. During the first two stages, Caltech researchers developed the construction concept, worked out the engineering design, and verified its operation in laboratory experiments on Earth. The team then had less than 12 months to manufacture, test, and deliver the space hardware to Momentus Inc., the company hosting the payload.

"Developing a payload of this complexity on such a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for our small team," says Pellegrino, who is also co-director of the Space Solar Power Project, which aims to harvest solar power in space and wirelessly transmit it to Earth's surface. "As we wrap up the mission, we are finally able to start thinking about the new avenues of research opened by this demonstration."

Why Scientists Want to Build Enormous Structures in Orbit

The ability to assemble large structures directly in space could transform astronomy, communications, and space based energy systems.

For example, future telescopes could use enormous reflective surfaces to collect more light and observe extremely distant objects. Similar structures could also support powerful radio antennas, allowing scientists and engineers to build communications systems much larger than those that can currently be launched.

One of the greatest obstacles is the limited room available inside a rocket's fairing, the protective enclosure that surrounds its payload during launch. No matter how ambitious a spacecraft design might be, its components must somehow fit inside that confined space.

Traditionally, engineers have addressed this problem in two ways. They either fold large structures into compact packages that can unfold after reaching orbit, or they launch separate components and have astronauts assemble them in space. Both approaches impose practical limits on the size and complexity of the finished structure.

Robotic construction offers a third possibility. Instead of fitting an enormous telescope or antenna inside a rocket, engineers could transport its materials into orbit and assemble the complete system there.

DARPA's Plan for Kilometer-Scale Space Structures

DARPA established NOM4D in 2022 to investigate technologies that could eventually "ferry raw materials from Earth for in-orbit manufacturing," according to the program's website.

Caltech's ASTRA experiment is one of only two projects selected to advance to the program's third phase, which involves demonstrating construction technologies in orbit.

The other project, led by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, will use a module attached to the International Space Station to investigate a technique for hardening carbon tubes in space. This could provide another way to manufacture structural components without having to complete every step on Earth.

"NOM4D's objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space," said Andrew Detor, DARPA program manager for NOM4D, in a written statement. "By 'very large,' I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today."

Such structures could eventually be several football fields long or even extend for kilometers, far beyond the dimensions of conventional spacecraft.

How Caltech's Construction Robot Reached Space

ASTRA began its journey on March 30, 2026, when a SpaceX Transporter-16 mission launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California early that morning.

The robot traveled aboard Momentus Inc.'s Vigoride 7 orbital vehicle, which carried 10 separate payloads into low Earth orbit. ASTRA occupied approximately one cubic meter of space, a compact package containing both the assembly machinery and the materials required for construction.

Inside were two previously assembled truss bays, reinforced with diagonal tubes and connecting joints. The payload also included a robotic arm and motorized dispensers loaded with the parts needed to construct the remaining sections.

The successful launch was an emotional moment for the small engineering team watching from Earth. Jaden Suh, a former Caltech postdoctoral scholar who is now an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin, was moved to tears as the spacecraft carrying his team's work headed into orbit.

"As a child, I was super curious about and interested in space structures. Just like many other engineers working in this field, sending your stuff to space is what I've been dreaming of my entire life," Suh says. "I was extremely lucky to have the opportunity to work on this project, beginning from scratch. A lot of my original ideas are included in this system, and it was just incredible seeing it reach space."

Building a Structure Hundreds of Miles Above Earth

After ASTRA reached orbit, researchers began operating the system by transmitting instructions to its onboard computer through the Vigoride spacecraft.

The initial steps involved releasing the mechanisms that had secured the components during launch. The robot then extended the two previously assembled truss bays out of the machine and proceeded to construct a third bay using the onboard assembly system.

Three team members managed the construction commands from Earth: Charles Sommer, a former Caltech systems engineer; Alan Truong, a Caltech research engineer; and graduate student Tara Venkatadri (MS '24).

Although the robot carried out the assembly operations automatically, the researchers monitored its progress using photographs transmitted from orbit. When something went wrong, they examined the images, adjusted their instructions, and attempted the operation again.

These setbacks were an important part of learning whether the technology could function outside a controlled laboratory.

"That's basically the reason you do proof-of-concept testing. There are a lot of differences in the space environment compared to down on Earth," Suh explains. "There are always lots of little surprises."

To diagnose problems in orbit, the engineers relied on a second ASTRA system kept at Pellegrino's laboratory at Caltech. This backup unit, known as a flight spare, allowed researchers to recreate difficulties encountered by the spaceborne robot and experiment with possible solutions.

"Every time we confirm there is an issue in space, we come to the laboratory and try to mimic the problem on the ground," Sommer says.

Communication restrictions made troubleshooting especially challenging. The team could contact ASTRA only during approximately seven or eight brief periods each day, with each opportunity lasting about 15 minutes.

That meant engineers had to make the most of their limited communication windows. They used the laboratory twin to investigate problems, evaluate different solutions, and determine which adjustments were most likely to work. Once a solution was ready, they sent the revised instructions to the robot in orbit.

This process helped the team work through numerous unexpected difficulties while gathering valuable information about what future autonomous construction systems will need to operate more reliably.

ASTRA's intended construction process involves repeating a carefully coordinated series of movements.

First, the robotic arm retrieves structural components from their storage dispensers. It positions the tubes and joints on an assembly plate and connects them to create a new truss bay.

Once the framework is assembled, the robot is designed to attach a thin reflective film containing many tiny openings. This material forms two reflective cable nets that are held under tension against one another by springs, helping the resulting surface maintain its intended shape.

The special film was jointly invented by researchers at Caltech and the University of Pennsylvania, where the collaborating team was led by Professor Igor Bargatin.

Unlike the knitted metallic mesh typically used in reflectors designed to fold and unfold, the perforated film requires less tension to maintain its shape. That allows engineers to reduce the amount of supporting structure needed, potentially making the entire assembly substantially lighter.

Lower weight is especially valuable in space engineering because every additional kilogram increases the demands placed on a launch vehicle.

When a bay is finished and its reflective components have been prepared, the robotic system pushes the completed section outward into space. It then begins assembling the next bay.

The full ASTRA antenna design calls for 11 connected bays, each attached to the reflective nets and extended outward from the assembly system.

A Small Demonstration With Enormous Implications

Despite successfully demonstrating the construction technique, the researchers do not expect ASTRA to finish assembling all 11 bays before the mission concludes in December.

The experiment has revealed several ways the robotic hardware and assembly procedure could be simplified and improved. Even without a completed antenna, the team believes it has collected enough evidence to establish that the approach is technically feasible.

The implications extend well beyond the relatively small antenna used in this demonstration.

Future robotic construction systems could help scientists build gigantic space telescopes that collect more light, radio antennas capable of supporting advanced communications, and enormous solar arrays designed to capture sunlight in orbit.

Such solar power systems could potentially transmit collected energy wirelessly to receivers on Earth, an idea being explored through Caltech's Space Solar Power Project.

More broadly, the successful test suggests that the size of future space infrastructure may not always have to be dictated by the dimensions of the rockets used to launch its components.

"Once you get to the size limit where structures cannot be prebuilt on the ground and unfolded, you have to think about how to build them in space," Pellegrino says. "So, this work could be useful not only for astronomy and astrophysics but also for communications and other areas, such as building very large solar arrays for space solar power."

#4338. Arc Raiders' new map will be unlocked through a community event that starts today, and everyone has to donate

It looks like it's going to take the Arc Raiders community a bit of work to unlock the game's next map.

As many of Arc Raiders’ regular players predicted, the game’s first post-launch map won’t just be available for everyone, it will instead be closely tied to a community event. Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

The event kicks off today alongside the release of the game’s latest patch. The ask is relatively simple: players must commit Basic Materials to the project so that the tunnels can be rebuilt. This option will be available to anyone who’s played at least five rounds.

If you’ve spent any time in Arc Raiders, you’ll know that Basic Materials are things like Metal parts, Fabric, Chemicals, Rubber Parts, and Plastic Parts - most of which are easy to find in the game’s various maps.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the new map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a new progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

Developer Embark describes the new environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the new map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The update will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap update will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

In case you’re still missing them, here’s how to find lemons and apricots, prickly pear, and olives.

#4337. Forgotten Memories: Definitive Edition is now free forever on iOS and Android

Free forever is a big promise, but Psychose Interactive has a fairly good reason for making it. Forgotten Memories: Definitive Edition, the studio’s survival horror from 2015, is now free on iOS and Android. No, this isn’t a weekend giveaway or one of Epic Games' weekly freebies. It’s staying that way.

You play as Rose Hawkins, who wakes up in an abandoned asylum while searching for a missing girl called Eden. It’s slow, third-person 90s-style horror, with puzzles, a torch and never quite enough ammo.

The asylum is split into different wings, and most of your time will be spent figuring out which locked door to open next. Our original review compared it closer to a point-and-click adventure, and with that many keys and locked doors, it’s probably true. The scares tend to land on the way back, once you’ve got what you came for and have to walk past the mannequins again.

It’s properly old-fashioned about the rest. You fight with a lead pipe and a bit of timing, and the torch battery runs down. Saving originally meant finding a computer and spending one of a limited stock of floppy disks, in the style of early Resident Evil, so dying could cost you half an hour.

Forgotten Memories: Remastered smooths some of the bugs out. It’s the rebuilt version that launched on mobile two years ago, with new lighting and checkpoint saves.

If the free one gets under your skin, the sale is the cheap way up. The Definitive Edition is free now on the App Store and Google Play. Forgotten Memories: Remastered is US$1.99 instead of US$6.99 on the App Store until Friday, November 13th.

A good chunk of our list of the best horror games on Android still charges for admission.

#4336. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Review: A Modern Remake With an Old Soul

Nintendo brings one of gaming's most influential adventures into the modern era without losing the magic that made it special.

I don't think I'll ever forget the first time I played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Not because I remember every detail of that first adventure, but because it was literally the first video game I ever played.

I was just a little kid who barely understood English, sitting in front of a Nintendo 64 with a controller (which, yes, wasn't even connected to the console because I was the younger sister) and a dictionary by my side. I had no idea what half the characters were saying, but I knew I wanted to see what happened next. Nearly 30 years later, I find myself returning to that same adventure, this time with a much better understanding of English and a controller that actually works. And, surprisingly enough, I think this might be one of the most emotionally powerful experiences I've had with a remake in a long time.

From Darksiders to Shinobi: Art of Vengeance, I present to you ten action-adventure games that are unexpected masterpieces.

Sure, we all know how revolutionary Ocarina of Time was back in 1998. Its approach to 3D level design, exploration, combat, and storytelling helped shape the entire industry, establishing a reference that countless games would follow for decades. But this remake doesn't seem interested in proving that all over again.

So, rather than trying to reinvent one of gaming's most influential adventures, Nintendo seems much more interested in touching something deeper than any groundbreaking mechanic ever could: the memories we built with this little boy, his fairy, and a world that once felt impossibly big.

For starters, let's get one thing out of the way: despite Nintendo's pre-release marketing describing this as a ground-up remake a few times, don't expect something along the lines of Square Enix's Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy. This is actually a faithful recreation of the original, much closer in spirit to what Nintendo did with Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask on the Nintendo 3DS.

The main story remains practically untouched, the overall structure is familiar, and most of the changes come in the form of visual improvements, quality-of-life adjustments, and a handful of additions that make the experience feel more modern. This means that if you've played the original, you'll recognize almost everything here.

And I can understand that this might disappoint some people. When a remake is announced as being built from the ground up, it's natural to expect substantial changes, perhaps even a new interpretation of familiar locations, mechanics, or story moments. But I think it all comes down to what you expect from this particular adventure in the end.

If you've played the original, you'll recognize almost everything here.

As a longtime Zelda fan who literally learned how to play video games with Link, I found this approach much more effective than I initially imagined, since it allowed the remake to strike a point much deeper than any new fancy level design could ever reach, largely because it understands that Ocarina of Time doesn't need a completely different story to make us feel something all over again.

Instead, it gives us that very same story with a series of carefully considered tweaks. Some are immediately noticeable, while others are the kind of little details you might not even realize have changed until you've spent a few hours exploring Hyrule again. And there's no better place to start discussing these changes than with the story itself.

If you've somehow never experienced Ocarina of Time, here's the short version: you're a little boy without a fairy who happens to oversleep one morning, only to be awakened by a very concerned fairy named Navi. Before long, you're thrown into a journey to save the world, involving a mysterious princess and an evil Gerudo king.

It's a wonderfully straightforward premise that gradually evolves into something much bigger, exploring themes of childhood, growing up, loss, and how the passage of time feels bittersweet for us all. And, nearly three decades later, its emotional impact remains remarkably intact. However, the remake introduces something that makes these familiar moments feel considerably more powerful: dedicated cutscenes with voice acting.

The original Ocarina of Time did an incredible job with the hardware limitations of the Nintendo 64. Seriously, the developers managed to create some wonderfully expressive moments with not much to work with back then. But now, these scenes finally have the cinematic presentation they've always deserved – and boy, does it make a difference!

I honestly lost count of how many times I caught myself wearing the dumbest smile while watching a cutscene. Seeing Princess Ruto slowly abandon her grumpy attitude as she falls for Link, watching Darunia dance to Saria's Song as if he's attending the greatest concert of his life, or witnessing the moment we realize Ganondorf only managed to obtain the power he wanted because we essentially fell for his little scheme.

These scenes have so much more personality now, and the voice performances help give familiar characters a newfound sense of life. More importantly, they made me realize something rather unexpected: deep down, these were already the scenes I had imagined back in 1998. As a child, we had essentially created a full version of these moments in our heads, but the remake gave those childhood interpretations a proper visual and emotional form, and that's a pretty wonderful achievement!

More importantly, they made me realize something rather unexpected: deep down, these were already the scenes I had imagined back in 1998.

And speaking of giving familiar characters more room to breathe, there's another storytelling improvement here that I absolutely love: how NPCs are way more important now.

The remake's dev team included younger folks, several of whom never played the original Ocarina of Time, who provided a much-needed modern view of things.

One of my favorite things about Ocarina of Time has always been its worldbuilding. Hyrule is filled with strange, charming, and occasionally downright questionable people, each with their own little stories and quirks. But the remake takes this aspect of the original and expands it in a surprisingly meaningful way.

Here's a tiny detail that makes a huge difference around here: time now passes continuously within Hyrule's towns. Basically, in the original, the world essentially had four different environmental states: Child Link during the day and night, and Adult Link during the day and night. This allowed certain characters and events to appear depending on the time period and Link's age, but the system was somewhat restrictive because time wouldn't actually progress while you were exploring towns.

Now, the remake changes that! The sun rises and sets naturally as you explore even inside cities, with characters appearing and disappearing according to their own schedules (except in more contained areas such as temples and minigame shops).

It's a small adjustment that makes the towns feel much more organic, almost as if their inhabitants finally have their own agendas, which gives it a lovely Majora’s Mask vibe. Also, this adds additional events and dialogue associated with these new day-night cycles, giving us more opportunities to learn about people we previously knew very little about.

My favorite example of this is Grog, who is arguably one of the saddest characters in the entire game. Remember that punk-looking guy who sits beneath a tree in Kakariko Village at night, complaining that everyone he knows is disgusting? In the original, we only really encounter him twice: once as Child Link and later in the Lost Woods as Adult Link. Well, thanks to the new time system, you can now find him walking around Kakariko Village during the day, too. And he has more dialogue and new interactions, finally giving more weight to fan theories that have circulated about him for nearly 30 years!

And this isn’t an isolated example. Several other characters receive similar attention, making Hyrule feel like a much more interconnected place. I absolutely love this kind of addition because it doesn't just give us more content for the sake of having more content. It actually enriches a world we already know, rewards longtime fans who have spent years discussing its little mysteries, and makes its characters feel like actual inhabitants rather than people waiting for Link to show up. It just makes everything feel a little more real.

Okay, so the remake has the storytelling side covered. But what about the actual gameplay? After all, Ocarina of Time wouldn't have become such an influential title without its approach to exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving.

The good news is that the core experience remains remarkably faithful, although there are plenty of quality-of-life improvements that make returning to Hyrule considerably more comfortable.

For starters, the item menu has been reduced to three main tabs, with a much cleaner organization that makes finding and equipping things considerably easier. I have to admit that I wasn't particularly fond of the menu taking direct inspiration from Breath of the Wild, since different games have very different needs. However, the new quick-access carousel is an absolute lifesaver, and switching between items during exploration and combat feels much more fluid. You no longer have to spend quite so much time navigating menus just to equip something.

And there's also a second quick-access system dedicated to some of your most essential tools, including the Ocarina, Lens of Truth, Happy Mask Salesman's masks, and (yes, you can finally celebrate!) the Iron Boots. This last addition is particularly welcome because it addresses one of the most infamous frustrations of the original game: the Water Temple.

But don't think everything is perfect just because most changes are improvements. Some of the modernized design decisions have introduced a few restrictions that, to be completely honest, I'm not entirely convinced were necessary. For instance, certain pieces of equipment have been tweaked to prevent players from using them in ways the developers seemingly never intended.

This happened with the Hookshot, which was previously a wonderful tool for experimenting with different traversal possibilities, but now only attaches to specific designated surfaces. That means you can no longer use it to reach rooftops, for example. Does this force you to find alternative solutions? Sure. But it also takes away some of the creativity and freedom that made experimenting with the original game's mechanics so much fun.

Still, this is where expectations come into play again. And there is something important to highlight: overall, the remake makes your life considerably easier than it was back in 1998, which means that finding new solutions isn’t actually hard. Around here, NPCs offer more hints and several sequences have been optimized to deliver a more straightforward experience. Oh, and there's also a dedicated quest log that helps you keep track of both the main adventure and your secondary objectives.

While I wasn't particularly happy about the Hookshot changes, I never felt like they significantly compromised my experience. Finding alternative solutions was generally okay, and the improvements elsewhere made the overall gameplay feel much smoother. So it's a trade-off, and one that I think works more often than it doesn't.

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

Now, here's where things get a little more complicated. As you might expect from a remake that's practically a 1:1 recreation, exploration remains very faithful to the original. And while the quality-of-life improvements make moving around Hyrule much more pleasant, they don't necessarily change how you interact with the world itself.

There are some additional visual indicators to help you find interesting things, though. Poes in Hyrule Field are now associated with specific fences, and Lake Hylia is no longer “separated” from the field, for example, making some environmental details easier to identify locations worth investigating. But the overall level design is pretty much what we experienced back in 1998, for better or worse.

And I have mixed feelings about that. On one hand, revisiting these locations with modernized controls and an entirely new visual presentation is an incredibly emotional experience. I genuinely enjoyed wandering around places I hadn't seen in years, recognizing familiar spots, and discovering little details that I had completely forgotten about. It's the kind of experience that makes you want to stop every few minutes just to appreciate how much care went into recreating this world.

On the other hand, I can't help wondering whether the developers could have gone a little further, especially since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom have completely changed our expectations of what exploring Hyrule can mean, giving us approximately 984,396 things to discover while traveling from point A to point B. Compared to those experiences, Ocarina of Time's more structured approach can feel a little restrictive, particularly when you know exactly where everything is supposed to be.

I would have loved to see a few more surprises along the way, perhaps additional secrets or expanded areas that rewarded players for approaching familiar locations from a different perspective. But, once again, I need to consider what this remake is trying to accomplish. As someone with an almost unhealthy amount of nostalgia running through my veins, I honestly didn't mind revisiting a place I consider home, even if the journey remained largely unchanged! However, if you're expecting a completely redesigned Hyrule with new exploration mechanics and substantially expanded areas, I'd recommend keeping those expectations in check.

Now, let's talk about the elephant in the room: the visuals. The remake retains the colorful, whimsical identity of the original, but practically everything has been reimagined from an aesthetic standpoint. Hyrule now looks even more like a fantasy world, with lush environments, intricate textures, expressive character models, and an almost overwhelming amount of environmental detail.

I have to confess that the new art direction took some getting used to. Kokiri Forest, in particular, initially felt a little too dense for my taste. Come on, don't any of these Kokiri kids own a lawn mower? And Young Link's redesigned appearance also gave me some mixed feelings during my first few hours.

But the more I played, the more the new aesthetic grew on me. Before I knew it, I was completely obsessed with how beautiful everything looked. And a big part of that comes down to the character designs. Rather than simply updating existing models with higher-resolution textures, the developers have reimagined several characters and enemies to better fit the remake's more elaborate fantasy aesthetic. The result feels cohesive, and there's a clear sense of inspiration behind practically every design.

Not to mention the little details! You can see (and feel, since this game is all about feelings, right?) just how much attention went into recreating familiar locations. Kakariko Village's well, for example, now features carefully rendered water and a variety of textures that make the environment feel considerably more tangible. Even something as simple as watching Link play the Ocarina becomes a visual treat, since you can actually see his fingers moving to the correct notes.

Also, the developers clearly know which details longtime fans care about. One particularly memorable example is how they've handled one of the game's most terrifying creatures (you know who!), since it is scarier than ever. And several bosses have also received additional visual details and updated animations that make their encounters feel more imposing.

And it's these little touches that make the difference! The remake doesn't just want Hyrule to look prettier; it wants every familiar corner to feel worth revisiting. And, honestly, I could spend hours just walking around and appreciating it all.

Putting everything together, I think it's fair to say that this is a remake that successfully modernizes a classic without losing its old soul. And considering how heavily nostalgia has influenced the gaming industry lately, with remakes and remasters seemingly arriving every other month, it's nice to see one that understands exactly what made its source material so special.

Most of the improvements are welcome, even if a few decisions (sorry, I still won't forgive what happened to the Hookshot) leave something to be desired. The updated gameplay makes the experience feel much more accessible, the visual overhaul is gradually gorgeous, and the additional storytelling touches give familiar characters a newfound sense of personality.

Putting everything together, I think it's fair to say that this is a remake that successfully modernizes a classic without losing its old soul.

There are also several additions that I’m obsessed with, from hearing iconic characters speak for the first time to seeing long-standing fan theories receive more attention, not to mention the extra Ocarina mechanics that let you hum melodies into the microphone to play them. It's a collection of thoughtful changes that, when put together, makes this adventure feel surprisingly fresh without sacrificing what made it so memorable.

And that's precisely why I think this remake works so well for longtime fans. It doesn't ask us to forget the original or replace the memories we built with it. Instead, it gives us an opportunity to experience those same feelings again, now with a presentation and gameplay that feel right at home in 2026. But I also believe it works wonderfully as an entry point for newcomers! Despite its faithful structure, the modernized controls, expanded guidance, and quality-of-life improvements make the experience feel far less dated than the original. So you can still appreciate everything that made Ocarina of Time revolutionary without having to deal with every limitation of a game released nearly three decades ago.

In the end, this remake made me feel like that little kid again, waking up early on Saturday mornings to spend hours exploring Hyrule, controller in hand (and, thankfully, connected this time). And I could feel that this was exactly what Nintendo wanted to accomplish within the first few minutes.

Playing this remake reminded me that video games can be much more than the mechanics we praise, the level design we analyze, the technical achievements we celebrate, or framerates that we fear to drop. Sometimes, their greatest power lies in how they make us feel, even decades after we've first experienced them – and Ocarina of Time still has that magic. Now, if you'll excuse me, I still have a few Golden Skulltulas and Heart Pieces to collect. And then? Well, I think I'm ready for another adventure.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

Zenless Zone Zero's 2.4 update is a chunky one, adding a new faction to the action RPG's roster alongside a new area, and fresh playable characters.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program was a big one, bringing us all the news about Version 2.4, the next major update. It’s called On the Precipice of the Abyss, and it will be available to download on November 26.

On the Precipice of the Abyss has tendrils in many areas of the game, touching several parts of its fiction as well as gameplay, so it’s one to watch out for.

Version 2.4’s biggest claim to fame is the introduction of the Krampus Compliance Authority, a new faction that’s affiliated with TOPS. This looks to be the oversight committee, dispatched after the squad’s adventure beneath Timesworn Hill.

The events of this narrative arch follow on from the Timesworn Hill crisis, which is partly why we’re going to a new area as part of this update. The old mining site can now be explored for the first time in a decade, now that the Miasma has begun to recede.

Our newcomers this time around are Dialyn and Banyue. Dialyn is an S-Rank Physical Stun Agent who’s a former customer service specialist. This isn’t just a backstory, however, as it plays into her gameplay.

Dialyn relies on two resources: Customer Complaint and Positive Review, but her core role is to stun enemies and allow teammates to unleash their Ults, with a nice boost to boot.

Banyue is another S-Rank, though he’s a Fire Rupture Agent. He uses his martial arts expertise to create combinations of might and grandeur. In combat, he pulls from Adrenaline and Wrathful Fires, alternating between the two to fuel his actions. There’s a bit of rhythm to his gameplay that might take you a little while to master.

Birkblick is Krampus' own proprietary lil bunny fella, who brings a sensor array that can transform into a cannon in combat, essentially tracking and immediately nuking targets. Then there’s Bild N. Boolok, a Support Agent-affiliated Physical damage dealing Bangboo bringing a giant block hammer to the fight to, well, smash enemies with.

It’s a bit of a winter party in Version 2.4, it seems, as the update will bring back Hugo (Attack - Ice), and Ellen (Attack - Ice), too.

You can also look forward to the return of the Bangboo auto chess event, which now includes PvE stages with unique rewards. In fact, playing this event is how you could get Bild N. Boolok for free. Lightstream Notes is another event that will be available for the duration of this update, and it will let you tag along with Ye Shunguang to New Eridu.

#4333. Rocket Rally brings 30-second arcade rally races to iOS and Android

You've got half a minute and one thumb to win

When we reviewed Major Mayhem, the iPhone 4S was brand new. Rocket Jump, the studio behind it, is back, this time with Rocket Rally, which is a physics-driven arcade rally racer that’s up for pre-registration on iOS and Android.

If it predates your phone, Major Mayhem was a one-finger cover shooter. Your soldier ran between cover by himself, and you held a finger down to fire. It was brash and silly and very easy to pick up for a minute, and it also earned a Silver Award from us.

Rocket Rally takes that one-input approach to rally. Races last thirty seconds, you play it one-handed in portrait, and the cars run on a custom arcade physics system the studio built itself. Time Attack and Head to Head sit alongside Rally X4 and Rally X6.

Around that is a solo career set in locations around the world, where you buy cars, upgrade them and build up a garage, plus daily online competition. There are over 100 stages across four environments at launch, with more promised every month, and hundreds of cosmetic options for your liveries.

Thirty seconds doesn’t feel like a lot, but I think it’s the right length for something like this. I don’t see myself completing a three-lap race on my phone while I’m en route somewhere, but a rally stage before my bus reaches its stop? I can see myself getting behind that. Of course, that means it leaves no time to learn handling that doesn’t make sense straight away.

Rocket Rally is expected to release on December 15th, although that could change. It will be free-to-play with ads. Pre-registration is currently open on the App Store and Google Play.

If you're into proper racing, most races on our list of the best racing games for iOS take a good deal longer than thirty seconds.

#4332. Battlefield 6 gets a new map today alongside major changes to controller aim assist, and even more weapon dispersion tweaks

Right on schedule, the latest Battlefield 6 patch has arrived to kick off the next stage of Season 1.

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other big new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Redsec players have a new Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

#4331. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising new approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

This connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Shows Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases."

Materials provided by Rockefeller University Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Players have used third-party applications to assist their play for years now, to mixed success and intent. Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

After unjustly banning a Battlefield 6 player, EA lost a court case to keep the ban in place.

Call of Duty: Warzone players have been utilizing one of the oddest forms of cheating I’ve ever heard of, peeking at the skill level of everyone in the lobby through the app Warzone Agent to decide whether or not to just leave the game. Activision has announced they’re clamping down hard on the practice, looking to eliminate it going forward.

Call of Duty players have been complaining about the franchise’s skill-based matchmaking (SBMM) for years now, a system where players are matched against foes equivalent to their skill level. This is, of course, how most matchmaking systems work, but COD players have been asking for its elimination since the original Modern Warfare remake.

In order to avoid these close matches, they utilize apps like Warzone Agent to figure out the average rank of the lobby before deciding to play, a practice Warzone’s anti-cheat division, Ricochet, has officially stood against. In their release surrounding the practice of lobby shopping, “moving forward, players who leave Warzone Agent loaded will not be able to access Multiplayer modes.”

Lobby shopping is the practice of hopping around warm-up stage lobbies to search for one with a lower skill ceiling, essentially targeting worse players to maximize your own boons. Activision has made it clear they won’t stand to suffer the practice any longer, further saying, “using unauthorized software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision Terms of Use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement.”

Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

Threatening to drop the ban hammer on violators is a great way to shake the practice off, and Activision isn’t stopping there, clarifying what it considers cheating. That includes external account boosting, led by swarms of bots they’ve managed to start stomping out.

Bots plague any free-to-play game people want to put time into, and focusing more on curtailing them is a great step toward slowing the flow, even if it is just a bandage over the wound. For now, Activision has drawn their line in the sand. The only question is whether or not they’ll flinch in the face of community complaints, but they’ve stuck by their guns this long.

The community complaint around skill-based matchmaking has always struck me as incredibly odd, with these players mostly desiring a true random selection process. These random matches are, on paper, more varied, but in practice lead to matches that are total stomps for one side or the other, leaving plenty of players with a bad taste in their mouths.

Getting to be the one stomping can be great fun, but that’s also possible against players of your skill level. SBMM’s main purpose is to minimize the games that feel like complete wipes from the loser’s perspective, keeping them playing against those who are actually equivalent to them on a broad scale. It’s far from perfect, but it's better than literally just tossing a random selection of players in a room.

Without it, not only would many casual players have to gamble on getting crushed every other game, but Activision could lose those players after enough rough matches, the true reason for the practice’s continued support. Despite the complaints, Activision has clearly long since decided that skill-based matchmaking is the best middle ground for skilled and casual players alike, giving everyone designated lobbies where they’re at least promised matches that are competitive.

Modern Warfare 4's launch party is still going, with a free play period for DMZ ready to rake in new players.

#4328. Here's The Best Graphics And Performance Mode For Phantom Blade Zero On PlayStation 5

Phantom Blade Zero is out now for everyone as a console exclusive on PlayStation 5 and on PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store as well. If you missed it, it's my favorite action game of the year so far, and you can read why in Game Informer's Phantom Blade Zero review. That explains why I think you should check the game out; Game Informer's list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks will get you some key information I wish I had when I started the game; and this guide I wrote up about the requirements you need to get the best ending in Phantom Blade Zero will help you find all story-critical content in the game.

However, you're looking for advice on which of the three visual modes Phantom Blade Zero offers you should use on your PS5. This here piece is for you.

Phantom Blade Zero has three visual modes on PS5 Pro: Quality, Balanced, and Performance. I tested all three. My personal favorite was Balanced, which gives you an upscaled (checkerboarded) 4K resolution at 40 FPS, as long as you have a 120Hz TV with VRR. If you have a 120Hz TV, it likely has VRR because most major manufacturers include it with 120Hz. I like this mode because the upscaled 4K looks beautiful, just a hair less than native 4K, and if you aren't someone super trained on those details, I'd wager you won't notice the difference. The best part is that this mode offers 40 FPS gameplay, which, contrary to how math works, is halfway between 30 FPS and 60 FPS; I'm not kidding, look it up. As such, 40 FPS feels much smoother than 30 FPS, and you're still getting crisp 4K resolution. It's a win-win for me and my go-to mode when a game offers it. That said, if you don’t have a PS5 Pro, you won’t see this Balanced mode.

The Performance mode offers an upscaled 2K resolution with a pretty locked 60 FPS. Phantom Blade Zero is an extremely fast, fluid action game, so I think many people will want the buttery smoothness of 60 FPS gameplay. If that's you, pick the Performance mode. Sure, its resolution is lower, and it will look blurrier and less crisp than the other two modes, but if you aren't switching back and forth often or looking at side-by-side images, you likely won't notice.

Quality mode is native 4K resolution (absolutely beautiful, the best visual image you can get playing Phantom Blade Zero), but at 30 FPS... and for a game like this, I don't think 30 FPS does it justice. I don't really recommend this mode for combat, but if you're just waltzing around Wulin, grabbing screenshots and such, turn it on and bask in the wonders of developer S-Game's art team. Note: There is an option for ray tracing on PS5 Pro. I tested all three graphics modes with it on and off and noticed zero performance changes or issues. So, use ray tracing – it’s nice!

#4327. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

If Redsec got you hooked on Battlefield gameplay but you never experienced traditional multiplayer in Battlefield 6, there's an upcoming moment you might want to pay attention to.

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

#4325. Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

The easier and more accessible Battlefield Studios makes those Battlefield 6 Challenges, the better.

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

#4323. Arc Raiders patch nerfs the Deadline mine, ends the menace of the Venator

The first post-Stella Montis patch for Arc Raiders has arrived, and it predictably touches much of what people brought to the latest map.

Arc Raiders has received a new update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance issues with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In today’s update, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

Check the official blog for the full change log for patch 1.3.0. If you’re just getting started with the hottest extraction shooter ever, our Arc Raiders tips offer plenty of help. You should also learn what all the different Map Conditions do in Arc Raiders, and how to best make use of each of them.

#4320. Battlefield 6 may have actually done it: beaten Call of Duty

Battlefield 6 sales are setting all kinds of records, but one in particular has long eluded the Battlefield series.

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.

This changes today, as the publisher - along with the game’s developer, PUBG Studios, have finally lifted the lid off the upcoming shooter.

Black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter. Squads of players infiltrate a mysterious island trapped in a time loop. There’s a bit of a STALKER element here with anomalies and various, unpredictable environmental shifts.

Coli, the island in question, hides a research facility that holds secrets and artefacts, which is what players will be attempting to extract. This is very much a PvPvE shooter, though PUBG Studios says the focus will be on exploration and discovery, rather than constant combat.

The game’s first set of closed alpha tests is set for December. The first takes place December 12-14, and another is scheduled for December 19-21. That’s six days across two weeks, with the test only being available on PC. Both sessions will be open to players in North America, Europe, and Asia.

As it usually works with these sorts of tets on Steam, the game’s Steam page has a link where you can request access. If granted, you’ll be able to find the closed alpha in your library and download it when the time comes.

Though this is a closed test, Krafton confirmed that players will be able to capture and livestream their gameplay. In fact, watching content creators might be how you get access, as Black Budget is going to have a Twitch Drops event running alongside those sessions.

When I played Arc Raiders prior to its launch, I likened its tense and uncertain atmosphere to that of the early days of PUBG, so it’s going to be very interesting to see what actual PUBG does with the extraction shooter premise.

So far, it sounds like it’s going to be doing its own thing, leaning more into the adventure side of the subgenre, but we’ll have to see how it all shakes out when the tests start. Indeed, the BR-like constantly shrinking circle sounds like it could be a game-changing twist.

#4316. Killing Floor 3 Studio Announces Layoffs After Publishing Hire Spree

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

Layoffs are always devastating for the video game industry and the people affected. Unfortunately, they have become all too common, and whether it’s a small studio or a large household name, it seems nobody is safe in today’s climate.

Tripwire Interactive, best known for the Killing Floor series, is the latest studio to be hit by layoffs. The studio was founded back in 2005, and Embracer Group acquired Tripwire Interactive through its former subsidiary, Saber Interactive, in 2022.

In our Killing Floor 3 Review, we go over what could have worked and what didn't in the end for Tripwire's latest game.

In a statement published on the official Tripwire Interactive X account, the studio says it “has undergone a workforce reduction, affecting 36 talented people across our studio. This was certainly not an easy decision, but unfortunately, a necessary one for the organization.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

The team will continue to focus on Maneater 2, which was officially announced as part of Sony’s September State of Play. It’s expected to launch sometime in 2027.

As the name suggests, Maneater 2 is the sequel to 2021’s Maneater, an action-packed RPG where you are the biggest threat in the open-world oceans that you’ll traverse. There are new evolutions, discoveries to be made, and a whole lot of opportunities to become the villain.

It has also been confirmed that work will continue on Killing Floor 3, as the developers try to salvage the rocky start the game had when it was released back in July 2025. Killing Floor 3 reviews remain mixed among critics and players, and updates are still rolling out, containing new content and fixes.

This isn’t the first time this year that Tripwire Interactive has held layoffs. On March 4, the studio cut its workforce by 23 people, meaning this new round of layoffs brings Tripwire Interactive’s total this year to 59. Only time will tell if any of Tripwire Interactive’s projects will suffer from delays as a result of these layoffs.

Similar to this instance, a real reason wasn’t provided for the March 4 layoffs, instead citing: “As the gaming industry continues to evolve, so do the needs of our studios, which means understanding our long-term strategy and aligning with business realities where needed in order to stay focused on our key creative goals.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

On November 4, 2026, Tripwire Presents, the publishing sector of Tripwire Interactive, announced that it would be expanding its business to include scaled publishing support for indie developers to help put the spotlight on indie titles from across a variety of genres. The purpose of the initiative is to provide greater visibility for self-published indie games that Tripwire believes fans will enjoy.

It has been confirmed that Tripwire Presents will continue to go ahead with their plans, and the games that have already been chosen are The Boss Gangster: Criminal Empire, Starforged Legacy, Mars Attracts, One-Eyed Likho, and Eslabong.

This round of redundancies adds another to the tally of alarmingly large video game industry layoffs just this year alone. Other examples include Sucker Punch making staff cuts shortly after the launch of the Complete Edition of Ghost of Yōtei, and, of course, the mass layoffs conducted by XBOX.

Another three rounds of XBOX layoffs are slated to begin this month and last into the new year.

#4315. d4v41 and Jinggg leave Paper Rex after 7th–8th Champions finish, Pacific place secure

Paper Rex has parted with captain d4v41 and Jinggg, two Masters Toronto winners, after an early exit at Champions 2026. With its VCT Pacific partner place secure, the Singapore organisation is rebuilding by choice as free agency opens to every region.

Paper Rex has broken up the core of its VALORANT roster. The Singapore organisation is parting with its captain and one of its best-known players as the 2027 season approaches. d4v41 had been with Paper Rex since its founding in 2020. He played first on its CS:GO roster, then moved with the team to VALORANT. Jinggg joined on 28 September 2021.

Neither player has named a destination. In the farewell video Paper Rex released, d4v41 said he was moving to a new team. Jinggg wrote on X that he was excited about what comes next. d4v41 also asked fans to keep supporting the organisation after both have gone.

The split follows a season that faded at the end. Paper Rex were runners-up at both Masters Santiago and Masters London earlier in 2026. At Champions in Shanghai, they lost 2-0 to LOUD in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 7 October. A 2-1 defeat to T1 in lower-bracket round one ended their run on 9 October. The event carried a $2,250,000 prize pool. LOUD went on to beat Team Vitality in the final.

The pair leave with a long record together. Jinggg helped Paper Rex to second place at Masters Copenhagen 2022. He was also part of the run to the Champions 2023 final, where the team were runners-up. Liquipedia lists both players in the line-up that won VCT 2025 Masters Toronto.

The changes are not forced by the league. The organisation is owned by IMPLS Entertainment Pte Ltd. Riot has cut the number of partner teams in each region from ten to eight for 2027–28. That leaves 32 across the four regions.

The Pacific format rewards that security. The eight partners receive seeded places at Kickoff in January 2027. Four further places go to teams that come through open qualifiers. Paper Rex can therefore reshape its roster without needing to qualify.

Two Masters winners on the open market could matter well beyond the Pacific. EMEA’s eight partners for 2027 are Fnatic, BBL Esports, FUT Esports, Team Heretics, Team Liquid, Gentle Mates, Karmine Corp and Team Vitality. Under Riot’s open qualifier rules, most regions require three of a team’s five players to come from that region. Teams must also keep three of five players between events to carry their progress forward. Those limits will frame how far any club can rebuild around new signings.
